the integration of the protein, gene and miRNA abundance data, as well as the DNA copy-number data, into our computational approach significantly outperforms previous approaches, and enables more accurate and reliable predictions of the growth inhibition patterns of novel cell lines and compounds.

We developed a computational approach that predicts the 50% inhibition growth endpoint (GI50) for a compound in a cell line by integrating the compound’s chemical structure and the cell line’s biological features (gene expression, protein expression, miRNA expression and copy number variation data).
We have developed a novel method to integrate the chemical and biological data to model the growth inhibition patterns of the NCI60 cell line panel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a computational approach to predict growth inhibition of cancer cell lines from a large number of compounds and cell lines.
the development of computational models for the prediction of growth-inhibition patterns of anticancer compounds.
the development of computational approaches to predict the growth inhibition of cancer cell lines by compounds and their potential to be effective against a range of cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of omics information to predict drug response is a promising approach, but that the data quality and availability of the data are critical for the success of the approach.
our approach provides the best possible prediction of the GI50 endpoint for a given compound and cell line combination, given the data available.
our model outperforms the previous ones in terms of predictive power and that, although the model is still not perfect, it is a significant improvement over the previous models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our models, which are based on a large-scale dataset of 59 cell lines, 17 142 drugs and 1.9 million GI50 values, can predict the growth inhibition patterns for new compounds on new cell lines.
the use of omics data, such as protein abundance, gene transcript and microRNA expression, can improve the prediction of growth inhibition bioassays in a large scale.

the integration of chemical, genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and miRNA data, as well as the use of a larger number of cell lines and compounds, can lead to a significant improvement in predicting the response of cancer cell lines to anticancer drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, within the limitations of the data, it is possible to predict the growth inhibitory effects of compounds against novel cell lines, tissues and compounds.

, in order to improve our understanding of drug sensitivity and to enable more effective use of anticancer therapeutics, we need to improve both the quality of experimental data and the quality of computational modelling approaches.
, although the NCI60 cell lines are not representative of the entire cancer population, they are still useful for the identification and validation of drug-pathway associations.
